title: Esther draws near and touches the top of the sceptre — in Brenton’s Greek the king lifts it and lays it on her neck
summary: KJV and Hebrew Esther 5:2 have Esther act: she draws near and touches the sceptre. Brenton’s Greek has the king act: he lifts the golden rod, lays it on her neck and greets her.
text: KJV Esther 5:2: “So Esther drew near, and touched the top of the sceptre.” Hebrew (WLC) Esther 5:2: וַתִּקְרַ֣ב אֶסְתֵּ֔ר וַתִּגַּ֖ע בְּרֹ֥אשׁ הַשַּׁרְבִֽיט [and Esther drew near and touched the top of the sceptre]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Esther 5:2 (Greek 5:2): 2 “Καὶ ἄρας τὴν χρυσῆν ῥάβδον, ἐπέθηκεν ἐπὶ τὸν τράχηλον αὐτῆς, καὶ ἠσπάσατο αὐτὴν, καὶ εἶπε, λάλησόν μοι. [And lifting the golden rod he laid it on her neck, and greeted her, and said, speak to me]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST05.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG05.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew has Esther approach and touch the sceptre the king held out; the Greek has no touch by Esther and gives the king the movements of lifting the rod, laying it on her neck and speaking. In the Greek the welcome is the rod laid on her neck and a greeting; in the Hebrew it is the sceptre held out and touched.
scope: T applies at Esther 5:2 only and compares who performs the gesture and what it is. It does not say the Hebrew and Greek accounts cannot both be true as one scene (the Greek has already told, at 5:1d–1f, that the queen fainted and the king came down to her), only that the wording differs. It does not say which text is original. The Greek of 5:1d–1f has no counterpart in the KJV. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew and Greek manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry. title: Esther “obtained favour in his sight” — Brenton’s Greek says God changed the king’s spirit to gentleness
summary: KJV and Hebrew Esther 5:2 say the queen carried favour in the king’s eyes (נָשְׂאָה חֵן). The Greek at 5:1e names God as the one who changed the king’s spirit to gentleness.
text: KJV Esther 5:2: “she obtained favour in his sight” Hebrew (WLC) Esther 5:2: נָשְׂאָ֥ה חֵ֖ן בְּעֵינָ֑יו [she carried favour in his eyes]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Esther 5:1e: Καὶ μετέβαλεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ βασιλέως εἰς πραύτητα, καὶ ἀγωνιάσας ἀνεπήδησεν ἀπὸ τοῦ θρόνου αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀνέλαβεν αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τὰς ἀγκάλας αὐτοῦ, μέχρις οὗ κατέστη· καὶ παρεκάλει αὐτὴν λόγοις εἰρηνικοῖς [And God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness, and in alarm he leapt from his throne and took her in his arms until she stood, and comforted her with peaceful words]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST05.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG05.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew gives no agent for the favour; the Greek gives God as the one who acts on the king. The Hebrew says what the king saw; the Greek says what God did.
scope: T applies at Esther 5:2 (Greek 5:1e) only. It compares who is named as acting. It does not say that the Hebrew excludes God’s action, that the Greek addition is later or earlier, or that the favour of the Hebrew is not understood as God-given. Brenton’s Greek names God in other places where the KJV does not (2:20, 4:8, 6:1, 6:13), already covered by the published record `god-named-in-the-greek-of-esther-where-the-kjv-names-none`; this record adds the one place where God is the actor on the king. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew and Greek manuscripts were not examined. title: Esther would have “held my tongue” — Brenton’s Greek has “I disregarded … the adversary is not worthy of the king’s court”
summary: The Hebrew has Esther say she would have kept silent had they been sold as slaves, because the adversary does not match the king’s loss. The Greek has her say she disregarded (something), because the slanderer is not worthy of the king’s court.
text: KJV Esther 7:4: “I had held my tongue, although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage” Hebrew (WLC) Esther 7:4: הֶחֱרַ֔שְׁתִּי כִּ֣י אֵ֥ין הַצָּ֛ר שֹׁוֶ֖ה בְּנֵ֥זֶק הַמֶּֽלֶךְ [I would have kept silent, for the adversary is not equal to the king’s damage]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Esther 7:4: καὶ παρήκουσα· οὐ γὰρ ἄξιος ὁ διάβολος τῆς αὐλῆς τοῦ βασιλέως [and I disregarded; for the slanderer is not worthy of the court of the king]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST07.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/7/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG07.htm.
reasoning: The two clauses start from the same sentence but give a different verb for Esther’s act and a different reason: loss to the king in the Hebrew, unworthiness of the king’s court in the Greek. The Hebrew sets a hypothetical (if only slaves, she would have kept silent); the Greek has an unexplained past act (παρήκουσα) and no “if”.
scope: T applies at Esther 7:4 only and compares the last clause. The Hebrew clause is difficult in every translation and the KJV rendering of “countervail” is itself an English choice. No lexicon was opened for παρήκουσα (a form of παρακούω) or for נזק, so the glosses are the researcher’s and could be narrower or wider than a lexicon gives. The record does not say the Greek mistranslates, nor that the two sentences cannot share one point (Esther would not have troubled the king for a lesser harm). A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew and Greek manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. title: The king “laid a tribute upon the land, and upon the isles of the sea” — Brenton’s Greek has him write upon the kingdom of land and sea
summary: KJV and Hebrew Esther 10:1 say the king set a levy (מַס) on the land and on the islands of the sea. Brenton’s Greek says the king wrote upon the kingdom of the land and of the sea; there is no levy and no islands.
text: KJV Esther 10:1: “laid a tribute upon the land, and upon the isles of the sea” Hebrew (WLC) Esther 10:1: מַ֛ס עַל־הָאָ֖רֶץ וְאִיֵּ֥י הַיָּֽם [a levy [was set] on the land and the islands of the sea]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Esther 10:1: Ἔγραψε δὲ ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐπὶ τὴν βασιλείαν τῆς τε γῆς καὶ τῆς θαλάσσης [And the king wrote upon the kingdom, both of the land and of the sea]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST10.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/10/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG10.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew states an act of taxation or forced labour on land and islands; the Greek states an act of writing about the kingdom with no object stated. The word for islands is not present in the Greek page.
scope: T applies at Esther 10:1 only. The Hebrew noun מס is rendered “tribute” by the KJV; it can mean forced labour or a levy, and no lexicon was opened here, so the record does not fix its sense. It does not say what the king wrote, whether the Greek reflects another Hebrew text, or which verse is original. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew and Greek manuscripts were not examined. title: Mordecai “was next unto king Ahasuerus” — Brenton’s Greek says he “succeeded” (διεδέχετο) king Artaxerxes
summary: The Hebrew calls Mordecai מִשְׁנֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ, “second to the king”. The Greek uses the verb διαδέχομαι with the king as object, a verb that in many texts means “succeed, take over from”.
text: KJV Esther 10:3: “Mordecai the Jew was next unto king Ahasuerus” Hebrew (WLC) Esther 10:3: מָרְדֳּכַ֣י הַיְּהוּדִ֗י מִשְׁנֶה֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹ֔ושׁ [Mordecai the Jew [was] second to the king Ahasuerus]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Esther 10:3: Ὁ δὲ Μαρδοχαῖος διεδέχετο τὸν βασιλέα Ἀρταξέρξην, καὶ μέγας ἦν ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ [But Mordecai took over from [succeeded] king Artaxerxes, and was great in the kingdom]. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/EST10.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/17/10/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/ESG10.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew places Mordecai in the second rank under a living king; the Greek verb, read in its common sense, makes him the king’s successor or deputy. The royal name also differs (Ahasuerus against Artaxerxes), covered by a published record.
scope: T applies at Esther 10:3 only and compares the rank statement. διαδέχομαι is also used of one who takes over a task or office from another while the first still reigns, and no lexicon was opened here, so this record does not say the Greek makes Mordecai king. The royal name difference is already covered by `king-ahasuerus-in-esther-or-king-artaxerxes-greek` and is not repeated.
